Paradoxe Studio

A browser studio that turns a one-sentence brief into a finished episode through thirteen observable stages (research, script, storyboard, shot pricing, generation, footage, motion graphics, music, subtitles, timeline, first cut, edit, export), in which Claude acts as the production team through declared tools while the person keeps three levels of control: automatic within a budget, collaborative with a gate at each stage, or manual. Edits from the agent and from the person share one nondestructive operation model with impact preview, locks, versions and undo.

Private. Walkthrough on request at support@lemonshops.app.How to useEngineering record

Engineering recordFor technical reviewers

Designed and built the whole studio: the production pipeline and its approval gates, the multitrack editor and its compositor, the audio engine and the licence model for music, the creative identity system, the prompt and skill library, and the phone layout. The hard part was letting an AI agent edit a real timeline without ever losing the person's work or spending money silently.

I type « cut the pause after the statistic » with the playhead as scope. The request goes to Claude with a summary of the project and the tools the studio declares; Claude answers with an edit_media call, a remove_range on the voice track. Before anything changes, the studio computes the impact preview: which clips shift, whether a locked scene is touched (it may not be) and the new duration. On approval the edit is applied as one undoable step, the activity log records it, the compositor redraws the frame and the waveform, and the project document is saved.

Key engineering decisions

01

A price before every generation

Each generated shot is priced with the provider's estimate before it runs. A budget of zero means the studio always asks; Auto Production spends only within the budget set for the project, and the monitor shows what has been spent.

02

The agent edits like a person

Edits from Claude go through the same operations as manual ones, are shown in an impact preview, respect locks and land as one undoable step. Nothing the person made is overwritten without a trace.

03

A reference is not a licence

A streaming link is stored as a reference with its licence status. It never plays under its name: a labelled original plays in its place, and the export either is publishable or carries a not-for-publishing mark.

04

Compose in short loops

Rendering a two-minute track as one audio graph froze the page. Rendering four to eight bar loops offline and tiling them made composition close to instant, and tempo detection now refuses to claim a tempo it is not confident about.

Notes for reviewers

Data modelA project document holds the brief, the plan (scenes, shots, claims), the timeline (tracks and clips), approvals, engine state and an identity snapshot; generation jobs are separate records keyed by project and scene, so a reload resumes them.
SecurityProvider accounts are connected by the user through authorised connectors; the studio stores no provider keys, and nothing paid starts without a price and an approval or a budget.
TestingA mocked connector layer returns research, plans and job states, including a job held at 42 %, so the monitor, the editor and the phone layout are tested without spending credits; one check caught a phone page that grew wider than the screen and hid the bottom menu.
Limits and next stepsServer-side rendering of final exports, multi-seat studios for creator networks, and direct publishing to each platform after checking which account is signed in.
01

Problem statement

A weekly talk show asks for the same chain every week: research with sources, a script written for the ear, a storyboard, footage or generated shots, music with the right to use it, captions and an edit. Off-the-shelf editors leave every step to the person; generative tools do the opposite, spending credits per attempt and replacing work wholesale. The design question was how far an AI agent can run a production while the person stays the author: able to see each stage, price each paid step before it happens, stop the agent at any gate, and never lose an edit to it.

02

Contribution

Three contributions. First, a production monitor that exposes thirteen stages and every scene with its cost, prompt, references, approval and lock, and three modes that move the gates without changing the pipeline. Second, a shared, nondestructive edit model: the agent's edit_media operations (remove a range, add a transition or an effect, adjust audio, regenerate a scene, apply the identity) and the person's manual edits pass through the same functions, are previewed for impact, respect locks and are undoable as single steps. Third, a licence-aware music layer: references and licences are distinct records, a reference never plays under its own name, a labelled original stands in, and export is either publishable or watermarked as a private preview.

03

Architecture

The client is written in plain JavaScript modules around one project document (brief, plan, timeline, approvals, engine state, identity snapshot). A Canvas 2D compositor renders video, stills, cards, captions and safe areas from the timeline model; MediaRecorder captures the export, and writers produce FCPXML and EDL for other editors. A Web Audio engine composes original music offline and analyses tracks. Claude receives a compact project summary and the tools the page declares, trimmed to the page's tool limit; generation and research providers (Higgsfield, vidIQ) are reached through MCP connectors the user authorises. Projects, jobs, music, prompts and identity live in a per-user document database, media in an asset store, and generation jobs are persisted so a reload resumes them.

04

Method and data

The engine runs the stages in order and stops at a gate when the mode requires it; generated shots are priced with the provider's estimate and approved individually or within a project budget. Original music is rendered as four to eight bar loops in an OfflineAudioContext at 32 kHz and tiled into full tracks, then encoded to WAV; tempo is estimated by autocorrelation of an onset envelope with a harmonic comb and a prior, and is reported only above a confidence threshold (the reference afrobeat sketch measures 112 BPM, an ambient bed reports none). Ducking lowers music under the voice; beat sync snaps cuts to detected beats. Identity uses a base plus overrides model, so changing a global default never alters a project that overrode it, and finished projects change only when the new defaults are applied explicitly.

05

Verification and limitations

Validation is scripted with Playwright over a mocked connector layer that returns research, plans and job states, including a generation held in progress at 42 %, so no credits are spent: 19 workspace checks at 1440 px, 16 navigation and phone checks, and layout checks at 390, 820 and 1024 px; an overflow audit found one phone page wider than the screen, which hid the bottom menu, and it was fixed. Limits: final exports are rendered in the browser, so long episodes depend on the device; music analysis is heuristic; a streaming reference can be documented but not licensed by the studio itself; publishing to each platform remains a manual step after the signed-in account is checked.
